newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican opposition seeks alliance to crush PRI.
newsitem.headline: Mexican opposition seeks alliance to crush PRI.

text.p: Critics of Mexico's ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party urged the country's divided opposition forces on Monday to unite to end the PRI's 67-year stranglehold on power.
In a newspaper advertisement, leading politicians and intellectuals called for the formation of a coalition to defeat the PRI in congressional elections in July.

"The proposal is to get the PRI out of the government," one of the alliance's founders, independent congressman Adolfo Aguilar Zinser, told Reuters in an interview. "For the first time in history, we have the votes accumulated by both (opposition) forces sufficient to create a new regime. Neither of them have the votes to do it alone."
It was not immediately clear whether the rallying call, published in the Reforma daily, would be heeded.
An official at the country's main opposition National Action Party (PAN) virtually ruled out any alliance with its rival on the left, saying it could unseat the PRI on its own.

"It would be a lamentable, historic error," Agustin Navarro, head of international affairs at the PAN, told Reuters, referring to an electoral alliance with the leftist Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD).
"Everytime the PAN has allied itself with the PRD it has won less votes than when it goes it alone."

The party of President Ernesto Zedillo has been in power since the Mexican Revolution, a regime sourly dubbed the "PRInochet" regime by some critics who paint it as resembling the long rule of the former Chilean dictator.
But during two years of painful economic crisis since Zedillo took office in 1994, many voters and even some officials have fled the party.

Analysts say the PRI could for the first time on July 7 lose its majority in the lower house of congress, the Chamber of Deputies -- a prospect that backers of the cross-party alliance want to make a reality.
"Mexico is at risk. Let's not waste time," said the paid advertisement by the "Alliance for the Republic."
Its proponents included Vicente Fox, a powerful figure in the PAN and governor of the central state of Guanajuato, and Rebeca Clouthier, daughter of a former PAN leader.

The proposal, Aguilar Zinser said, was accepted by PRD leader Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador, and aims to forge political principles common to both parties that would help Mexico through a transition period if the PRI loses Congress.
But the PAN appeared highly unlikely to play ball.
Navarro cited polls saying it could win more seats than the PRI in Congress and clinch victory in the race for mayor in Mexico City, the first time that post is up for ballot.
In the Mexico City race, he said popular PAN ex-presidential candidate Diego Fernandez de Cevallos could run, even though so far he has appeared reluctant.
"Keep that lottery ticket in your pocket," Navarro said.
